item.title: The Windows blue screen of death could have looked completely different if a 33-year-old decision had gone another way
item.itunes:title: The Windows blue screen of death could have looked completely different if a 33-year-old decision had gone another way
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The iconic blue screen of death (BSOD) has graced some of our worst Windows moments over the years —moments when your PC completely gave up. This error screen is reserved for catastrophic errors that prevent Windows from functioning normally. The OS displays the details of whichever process caused the fatal crash, and restarts itself to avoid damage to your data and hardware.

Interestingly, the Windows BSOD didn't have to be blue. The choice goes back to Microsoft engineers working on Windows NT who picked the color because it was familiar, not because it signified something important. The choice stuck for decades before Microsoft finally swapped blue for black in 2024, ending the three-decade legacy of the blue screen of death.

12 examples of how Windows BSODs can strike anywhere

Your PC ran into a problem again. :(

By  Rich Edmonds

The blue color was born out of convenience

Microsoft just winged it

  • Credit: Flickr
  • Credit: Flickr
  • Credit: Flickr
  • Credit: Flickr

The blue screen of death, as we know it, can be traced back to the development of Windows NT 3.1 in the early 90s. Microsoft developer John Vert was working on the NT kernel code that displayed the stop screen by switching the display into text mode and adding the error message on it. He picked the white-on-blue design of the BSOD that shipped with Windows NT 3.1 in 1993.

The reason behind the choice was practical more than anything else. The MIPS workstation he worked on used a white-on-blue color scheme for its firmware boot screen. Plus, the SlickEdit text editor used by many Windows NT developers at the time had the same default color scheme. He simply used the same design for the new Windows stop screen, so that it felt consistent and also easier to read.

If Vert's workstation had used a different default color scheme, the BSOD that we know would never have been blue. There were no brand guidelines or technical limitations behind the blue screen. It could have been black, like Windows 3.1's crash screen, or even green, as seen today on Windows Insider Preview builds.

Bill Gates called the famous key combo in Windows a mistake, and Microsoft never wanted you to use it

Three awkward keys, one accidental legend, and a very strange Windows history.

By  Yash Patel

Windows NT wasn't the first version to have a blue screen

But it was the first one to have a true BSOD

Credit: Wikimedia Commons

Curiously, even Windows versions before NT had featured blue screens, although they weren't technically stop screens or "screens of death." On Windows 3.1, pressing Ctrl + Alt + Del on the keyboard brought up a screen that allowed you to close a stuck program. It was written by Steve Ballmer, and Microsoft engineer Raymond Chen referred to it as the "blue screen of unhappiness."

A few years later, Windows 95's error screen, which Chen himself worked on, also displayed white text on a blue background. It allowed the user to either ignore the error and continue using the PC or restart the system. Later versions, like Windows 2000, XP, Vista, and 7, started giving more information on the BSOD to give users a clue about what had crashed the system.

Then, Windows 8 revamped the terminal-style, text-only look of the BSOD, giving users a different shade of blue, modern font, and a huge sad smiley. It also removed any additional information about the error, leaving people guessing. BSODs weren't as common by then, and Windows 10 continued the same look, but it added a QR code that users could scan for additional information.

4 beloved features from Windows history that Windows 11 got rid of

Out with the old, in with the...well, nothing.

7
By  Simon Batt

The BSOD hasn't been "blue" for a while

Black is the new blue

Credit: Wikimedia Commons

Sadly, the "B" in BSOD no longer stands for "blue" anymore, thanks to Microsoft making the change in Windows 11 24H2 back in 2024. It's now the black screen of death, if you want to be accurate. Although Microsoft had attempted the same transition in 2021, complete with the sad face and QR code, it rolled back to the familiar blue screen pretty quickly.

With the 24H2 update, however, the company committed to adopting the new BSOD to bring it in line with other modern Windows design choices. It cited a more streamlined UI as the motivation for the switch. The QR code and sad face were removed, and the text was simplified to "Your device ran into a problem and needs to restart." An error code remains at the bottom, accompanied by a progress counter above it.

Most users didn't seem to be fans of the "switch to black." It looks more like a Windows update screen rather than a fatal error screen. Talking about it is moot since it's been two years already, but it's worth pointing out that the blue screen of death wasn't just a visual choice. It had become synonymous with the times your PC ran into an unsolvable error, and the black screen just doesn't feel the same.

7 features Windows 12 needs to borrow from its competitors

Microsoft needs to take more than one note

23
By  João Carrasqueira

No one wants to see a BSOD, but blue is still better than black

Microsoft wanted to simplify the stop screen and changed it from blue to black. However, I believe the black screen of death is way more intimidating than what we had before. The blue theme was relatively calmer and didn't instill a sense of dread as the black screen does now. The old BSOD also didn't look like a Windows update screen, so there's that.

item.title: I trust plain text more than any app, because it still opens after every app is gone
item.itunes:title: I trust plain text more than any app, because it still opens after every app is gone
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
There are plenty of ways you can write down notes and documents on your PC, and we tend to be drawn to the ones that offer more features. Fancy formatting, syncing capabilities, and others can make it appealing to opt for a more advanced editor.

But when it comes to longevity and compatibility, plain text is, and likely will always be, the way to go. If I want to make a document I can always access in the future, plain text is what I'm choosing.

It works on everything

If it works in the terminal...

The thing about plain text files is that they've existed almost as long as computers themselves, and they work on basically anything. Windows opens them in Notepad, macOS opens them in TextEdit, and Linux has a wide array of text editors. In fact, you can even edit these files in the terminal using Nano or, on Windows, Edit. If you can edit a file in a terminal window and not lose any information, you know that file will work anywhere.

And it's not just that it works on any device, but you can really use these files on almost any program you want. If you're used to VS Code, you can keep opening them there, or most other IDEs. You can use programs like Notepad++ on Windows if you want a more advanced suite of tools to edit those files than the basic Notepad. Plus, all these tools that edit plain text are lightweight and very fast. In the time it takes to load Word, I can get a decent head start on my writing.

What's more, plain text can also go anywhere and not break things. When I have no internet but still need to get started on writing an article, I go to Notepad and put my words there. When I get a connection, I can just copy that content and paste it into the CMS, and I don't have to worry about formatting. Copying from Word or other text editors can cause a lot of weird issues with different online systems, but plain text always works.

I'm sick of proprietary notetaking tools when plain text is simply better

Fast, portable, future-proof note-taking

8
By  Nolen Jonker

Any single piece of software, be it Windows as a whole, Notepad, or VS Code could disappear, and I would still be able to open and edit these files wherever I want. That's the beauty of it.

We have syncing at home

I don't need a fancy editor for that

One of the many features you might get from more advanced text editors like Obsidian is the ability to keep those files synced across devices, but you don't need a fancy editor for that, either. You can store text files in a cloud storage service and make them accessible everywhere, though you'd still be dependent on having a client that can access that cloud service. On some platforms, like Linux, that can be harder.

Personally, I prefer using Syncthing, since it works on any device relatively easily, and it allows me to sync files without keeping them stored on any third-party server. I can either sync directly between my active devices, or use my NAS as a relay to keep files in sync across different devices. Syncthing keeps files in sync on the folder of my choice and lets it all feel local, so I never even think about it being a sync service. It's just working in the background.

I replaced the cloud with a spare laptop and Syncthing, and now my files sync for free

Who wants expensive monthly fees anyway?

4
By  João Carrasqueira

Formatting options are just flourishes

Nice to have, but optional

I understand the appeal of having nice formatting options to make things more easily readable, but frankly, I rarely find it necessary. Any formatting I really need can easily be signaled with plain text, and you can come up with your own methods to do it. Usually, if I need to be able to read a text file relatively easily, just using line breaks around headers is really all I need to be able to skim it. I may need an extra second to see the content of a header, but it works perfectly fine.

The only times where I care to use more advanced text editing programs if I'm working on something to share with others. Again, I understanding wanting something easier to read, so I generally try to create something more visually appealing if someone other than myself needs to look at whatever I'm writing. Plus, these programs let me create things like tables or insert images, which can sometimes be helpful.

This open-source Markdown editor is replacing every other writing app I use

When it's time to write instead of organize, MarkText is my first choice.

1
By  Yash Patel

Even then, you could argue plain text is still a great fallback, especially when you consider Markdown files, too. The main difference between a plain text file and a Markdown file is that if you open that file in a Markdown viewer, it can render the text with different text sizes based on your syntax.

There's nothing stopping me from creating a plain text file, using Markdown syntax to signify headers or tables, and then saving a copy with the .md extension to load it up with the appropriate formatting. Conversely, I can rename a Markdown file and change it to the .txt extension to see the syntax in plain text form to edit on any device, and it's still perfectly usable.

Plain text is still king on my PCs

It may not be the prettiest, but plain text documents are still how I go about a lot of my work. If I need to write an article but can't access the internet, that's where I go. When I'm taking notes to bring up during a meeting, I take them with Notepad or an equivalent. Plain text files work everywhere, every time, and they may still be around after the heat death of the universe. I can't ask for much better than that.

item.title: I turned my old Pixel into a USB webcam without installing a single app
item.itunes:title: I turned my old Pixel into a USB webcam without installing a single app
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My Pixel 8 has sat unused since I switched to my Galaxy S25 Ultra, and I was looking for a practical way to get it working again.

At the same time, I wasn’t particularly impressed with my laptop's built-in webcam. I considered buying a dedicated webcam, but then I found a handy Android feature on my Pixel that does the same job without third-party apps, complicated workarounds, or extra accessories.

A battered screen didn't stop me from turning my old Samsung phone into a functional home server

It's now an important part of my home lab

By  Abhishek Kumar Mishra

My old Pixel has a hidden talent

A useful feature hiding in plain sight

Ever since I switched to my Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra, I haven't used my Pixel 8 much. I occasionally pick it up to test new Android features, but otherwise, it spends most of its time sitting in a drawer.

As it turns out, Google introduced native USB webcam functionality that allows compatible Pixel phones to double as webcams for computers. The feature has been around for a while, but I completely overlooked it.

I was also surprised by the straightforward implementation. Unlike third-party solutions such as DroidCam, Google’s built-in option doesn’t require installing companion software on my Windows PC or Mac. It uses the standard USB Video Class protocol, so my computer can recognize the Pixel as a webcam.

Since my Pixel 8 still has an excellent camera system, leaving it unused while relying on an ordinary laptop webcam suddenly felt like a missed opportunity.

Setting everything up was quite easy

Just a USB cable and a few taps

As mentioned, Google made the process easy, and I had my old Pixel working as a webcam within minutes. I started by connecting my Pixel 8 to my Windows desktop using a USB-C cable. Make sure the cable supports data transfer, since a charging-only cable won’t work.

Once connected, I unlocked my Pixel 8 and pulled down the notification shade. I tapped the Charging this device via USB notification to open Preferences. Under Use USB for, I selected Webcam. I tapped the new Webcam notification to open the camera preview and adjust the framing.

Finally, I opened Google Meet on my desktop and selected Android Webcam as my camera source.

That was pretty much it. My Pixel was ready for video calls without needing any additional software on either device. I could even switch between the front and rear cameras and adjust the zoom directly from my phone.

I didn’t have to deal with wireless pairing, IP addresses, or complicated companion apps. The entire experience felt like plugging in a regular USB webcam, except I was using a smartphone I already owned.

The rear camera makes the difference

Google included handy controls

While my laptop’s webcam gets the job done, the Pixel has a much more capable 50MP main camera with a larger sensor and better optics. I started with the front-facing camera, which worked fine for regular video calls.

However, switching to the rear camera made the setup much more interesting. I could use the Pixel’s superior camera hardware to get a cleaner, more detailed video feed, especially when the lighting wasn’t ideal.

Of course, this doesn’t mean I get the same image quality as shooting a regular 4K video on my Pixel. The webcam feed has its own limitations, but it’s still a practical upgrade over relying on an ordinary laptop webcam.

Once I enable Webcam mode, I can tap the Webcam notification on my Pixel to launch a live preview. From there, I can switch between the front and rear cameras, use the preset zoom controls, or pinch the screen to fine-tune the framing.

There is also an HQ toggle to improve video feed quality. Another thoughtful touch is that I don’t need to keep my Pixel’s screen turned on throughout a meeting. Once I adjust the framing, I can lock the phone, and the webcam keeps working in the background.

The Pixel also charges through the connected USB cable, so I don’t have to worry about draining its battery during longer calls.

I put a Raspberry Pi inside my Nintendo 3DS, and now my PC sees it as a gamepad, webcam, and microphone

The DSpico can turn your DS into an impressive bag of tricks.

5
By  Adam Conway

It works beyond my Windows desktop

One phone, multiple computers, zero hassle

Another thing I appreciate about Google’s implementation is that it isn’t restricted to one specific platform. I frequently switch between my Windows desktop and MacBook Pro, so having a webcam that works across both platforms is a major advantage.

I can simply connect my Pixel, enable webcam mode, and select it as the camera source in supported apps like Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, and Zoom. In comparison, Apple’s Continuity Camera is excellent, but it requires an iPhone and a compatible Apple device.

The webcam upgrade I never expected

I wasn’t expecting my old Pixel 8 to become a permanent part of my desk setup, but this little experiment convinced me otherwise. The camera hardware is still capable, the setup is straightforward, and the results are good enough for my everyday video calls and meetings.

Sure, there are some limitations, but they are minor compared to the convenience. If you have a compatible Pixel collecting dust (or use one as a daily driver), try this feature before spending money on a new webcam.

item.title: I replaced my VS Code workflow with Google Antigravity, and cut my coding time in half
item.itunes:title: I replaced my VS Code workflow with Google Antigravity, and cut my coding time in half
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
While VS Code has served me well, I recently started wondering whether there was a faster way to handle complex coding projects. Instead of comparing features on paper, I decided to put Google’s Antigravity to the test.

I picked up a complex website project, started from scratch, and attempted to build the same thing using both tools.

I was amazed at just how capable Antigravity was and how quickly everything came together. By the time I finished, I had cut my development time nearly in half.

I used Claude Code, Google Antigravity, and Codex for a month and I have a clear winner for you

The search for the perfect coding assistant

32
By  Parth Shah

I stopped micromanaging every coding task

Antigravity understands what I am trying to build

Before I go any further, I want to clarify that I am comparing the default AI coding agents in VS Code and Google Antigravity. I’m not talking about using third-party solutions like Claude Code or Codex. For Antigravity, I am using Google’s Gemini 3.8 Flash model (Gemini 4 Argon wasn’t available at the time of writing).

Now, VS Code has come a long way with the Agents Manager view. However, I noticed a difference in how much attention the default agents required during my website project.

In VS Code, I often broke larger tasks into smaller instructions, checked the output, and sent follow-up prompts to get exactly what I wanted. The agent was capable, but I still felt like I was directing much of the process.

Antigravity felt more independent in my experience. For example, I could describe an entire dashboard with a sidebar, interactive charts, responsive layouts, and multiple pages.

I still reviewed the code and made corrections when needed, but the constant back-and-forth was reduced. That was the first major productivity improvement I noticed after switching.

Project setup stopped eating my time

Getting started became effortless

One thing I have always disliked about starting a new coding project is the initial setup. Before I can work on anything exciting, I need to decide on the framework, create the folder structure, install dependencies, configure the development environment, and make sure everything runs properly.

VS Code’s built-in agent can handle these tasks too, but I often find myself providing additional instructions. Antigravity made this process feel much more effortless.

It planned the project structure, created the necessary files, and configured the development server. I could review its progress and intervene when necessary, but I didn’t have to constantly jump between the terminal, file explorer, and AI chat.

My website came together in half the time

The little savings quickly added up

The biggest surprise came when I looked at the overall quality of the finished website. Compared to GitHub Copilot in VS Code, Gemini 3.8 Flash is a major improvement. I gave it one giant prompt describing the website’s structure, design language, features, navigation, and overall appearance.

To my surprise, it got nearly 80% of the work right on the first attempt. The initial output looked much closer to what I had envisioned, and I only needed to spend time polishing smaller details.

Copilot also did a decent job in VS Code, but the final output needed more tweaks and manual work than I had imagined. That extra work quickly added up.

That was where Antigravity made the biggest difference for me. I wasn’t necessarily saving time because Gemini wrote code faster. I was saving time because I had less work to redo. By the time I finished refining the website, my overall development time had dropped by nearly half compared with my usual VS Code workflow.

I tried agentic coding in Google Antigravity 2.0 for a week, and now standard IDEs feel like typewriters

This is coding on autopilot.

12
By  Parth Shah

Browser testing no longer felt tedious

Parallel agents kept my projects moving

Browser testing is another area where Antigravity impressed me. Now, VS Code already has a built-in browser, and its GitHub Copilot agent can interact with websites, run tests, and identify issues.

I am not suggesting that Antigravity introduced something completely new here. But I found Google’s implementation more convenient for my workflow.

For example, I could ask Gemini to open my website in Chrome, navigate between pages, confirm if the checkout workflow is working properly, and test interactive elements. I appreciated how Antigravity presented the results. It could generate screenshots and browser recordings as artifacts and gave me a visual record of what the agent had done.

Another area where Antigravity saved me time was handling multiple tasks simultaneously. VS Code’s Agents Manager also supports parallel sessions. However, I found Antigravity’s agent-first interface more intuitive for delegating work and reviewing progress.

However, this is one area where I want Antigravity to steal Devin Desktop’s Kanban board feature, where I can see all the agents' tasks in columns and take actions accordingly.

The productivity boost I never expected

I didn’t expect a single IDE switch to make such a noticeable difference in my coding workflow. After building the same website in VS Code and Google Antigravity, the biggest takeaway wasn’t just the time I saved, but how much less effort the entire process required.

Of course, VS Code isn’t going anywhere. It remains a reliable choice with a mature ecosystem and plenty of customization options. However, for complex projects where I want to move from an idea to a working prototype as quickly as possible, Antigravity has become my preferred choice.

item.title: Phone GPS is the worst way to do presence detection, and it's why most smart homes feel dumb at the front door
item.itunes:title: Phone GPS is the worst way to do presence detection, and it's why most smart homes feel dumb at the front door
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Some smart homes fail at the most basic of tasks, and that might be because your setup relies entirely on sluggish smartphone GPS geofencing. When you rely on the Home Assistant companion app or native platform geofences to track home vs. away states, you assume your phone GPS is enough to run an automated household. While your phone GPS is designed for navigating highways, it's not built to manage your doorstep. It suffers from massive latency, battery-draining polling intervals, and dead zones that leave you standing in the dark.

Real home automation requires spatial awareness rather than satellite coordinates. A much better alternative is macro-zone geofencing backed by local room-level presence, like ESP32 Bluetooth proxies and mmWave radar. This allows you to build an entry routine that feels genuinely intelligent rather than sluggish and slow.

7 ESP32 projects that replaced commercial smart home gadgets in my house with cheaper, local hardware

These are the commercial products I've replaced with ESP32-powered variants.

11
By  Adam Conway

Move away from phone GPS

By ditching raw GPS geo-fencing for front-door triggers, you can build a smart home that greets you the moment you arrive, not three minutes later.

item.title: Your SSD isn't old, it's slowing down for 3 reasons you rarely think about
item.itunes:title: Your SSD isn't old, it's slowing down for 3 reasons you rarely think about
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
So, you're one of the lucky ones who built a PC or upgraded your SSD way before the DRAM crisis exploded prices across the industry. Your NVMe SSD may have been blazing-fast when new, but you might feel that it has lost some of that speed over the years. It's not your imagination; SSDs can slow down over time if you aren't careful about upkeep and updates.

SSDs, just like other components of your PC, don't like heat. You may have a fancy heatsink installed on it, but that doesn't guarantee your drive will never throttle. SSDs don't need frequent firmware updates, but you may have missed out on a crucial one if you never checked for updates. Lastly, your drive needs to have enough free space to run background maintenance that keeps it performing at its best. Thankfully, each of these mistakes is easy to rectify.

Your SSD is running a multi-core computer with its own RAM, and that's the only reason it's fast

Without the controller and external DRAM, your SSD would lose its bragging rights

1
By  Tanveer Singh

Your drive is overheating inside a dirty case

You may not even realize it

I understand it isn't convenient to have to clean your case every few months. In dusty areas, your PC can accumulate dust deposits in a matter of months. At this point, the dust ruins the aesthetics of your build, but if ignored for too long, it can start to hamper the airflow inside your case. When your case fans get clogged with thick dust, they struggle to provide the passive cooling your SSD needs to avoid thermal throttling.

To be fair, NVMe SSDs don't throttle easily. Gen4 drives run fine till 70℃, and Gen5 drives are okay below 75–80℃. However, in the worst cases where you procrastinate deep cleaning for too long, your SSD can breach these safe limits under heavy load. When this happens, the same tasks that used to fly on your new drive will run relatively slower. You may not be monitoring your SSD temperature, so the root cause can go unnoticed.

Overheating isn't ideal for your SSD's lifespan either. NAND flash wear isn't the only thing that can kill your SSD; you also need to protect it from sustained overheating. If you keep ignoring your dusty PC for months on end, it won't be long before you start slashing your SSD's lifespan.

5 PC maintenance tasks I was doing wrong all this time

Fortunately, I fixed my mistakes before something went seriously wrong

4
By  Tanveer Singh

You haven't updated its firmware in ages

It's possible you never even thought about it

Your PC's BIOS needs to be up-to-date for optimum performance, stability, and security. Similarly, your SSD's firmware also needs to be updated to ensure you aren't missing out on performance improvements or critical security patches. Manufacturers don't push too many firmware updates for SSDs, especially not once the drive is a bit far into its lifecycle. That said, during the first few years, it's worth checking your SSD software for new firmware.

SSD firmware directly impacts the drive controller's performance. It sits below the OS and helps the controller and NAND flash execute important operations like garbage collection, wear leveling, and error correction. The overall result of these operations is a drive that maintains its peak performance for years. If you've never updated your SSD's firmware, you may be missing out on a performance-linked update.

A new firmware version isn't just linked to performance; it can also prevent early degradation. This was exactly what happened with early batches of Samsung's 980 Pro SSDs, where a firmware update prevented drive failures across the customer base. Hence, ignoring your SSD's firmware isn't advisable if you wish to enjoy your drive's maximum performance for years.

Ignoring SSD firmware updates can hurt performance and even your data

Your SSD's firmware is its soul that drives every critical operation

By  Tanveer Singh

It's running out of free space

Give your SSD some breathing room

You paid for every last GB of your SSD, so you may want to use it to the brim. That approach, however, isn't healthy for its performance. When your SSD is new, it has an abundance of free cells. Whenever you write new data to the drive, the controller doesn't need to hunt for an empty cell. As it gets filled up, however, this process can get slower, since the drive needs to erase existing cells by relocating data and then write new data to empty cells.

This process of cleaning up invalid or deleted data from cells and readying them for incoming data is known as garbage collection. An SSD that's running out of free space struggles to perform this process efficiently, which slows down write operations. It can also cause write amplification since the SSD has to perform extra write operations, reducing the lifespan of the drive.

The other problem with an SSD that's "too full" is that the pseudo SLC (pSLC) cache gets smaller. Without a sufficiently large pSLC cache, your SSD is forced to write natively to the TLC or QLC NAND, which is relatively slower. The small area reserved as the SLC-imitating cache uses spare space on the drive to dynamically adjust its size. With too few empty cells on the drive, your SSD struggles to find spare storage for the cache, making your SSD slower over time.

This is why it's advised to keep around 10–15% of your SSD capacity unused. This allows the drive enough free space to manage garbage collection and maintain a healthy pSLC cache for write operations. Ensure that the TRIM command is also enabled on Windows, so that the SSD is always up-to-date on which cells contain invalid data. This aids the garbage collection process, minimizing unnecessary writes.

I doubled my SSD endurance by changing these Windows settings

A few quick changes and you can heavily decrease your SSD's load

14
By  Ty Sherback

Your SSD's slowdown is probably not linked to its age

Fortunately, it's easy to regain the performance your SSD has lost over the years. Its age doesn't determine its speed; its cooling, firmware, and free space do. Once you've ensured your drive isn't throttling, is using the latest firmware, and has enough spare storage to manage background operations, you'll find it returning to its former glory.

item.title: I installed Debian on my Kindle, and it's now a pocketable terminal for my home server
item.itunes:title: I installed Debian on my Kindle, and it's now a pocketable terminal for my home server
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I jailbroke my Kindle a few months ago to use it for more than reading, like sideloading games and playing music. I figured kTerm would be enough to reach my self-hosted services and my Linux home server. But kTerm just opens a shell into a stripped-down BusyBox environment. It’s there to run the e-reader, not to act as a general Linux machine, and there’s no apt to pull in the tools I’d normally reach for on a server.

Running real Linux software on the Kindle meant waiting for someone else to cross-compile it first. I didn’t want just a terminal window into my home server, though. I wanted the Kindle itself to run Linux while still functioning as an e-reader. That sounded trickier, but a chroot made it happen.

I turned my old Kindle into a second monitor, and it's the perfect passive display for my desk

E-ink monitors cost $500+, so I built one from a spare Kindle with just Python and a weekend

By  Dhruv Bhutani

My Kindle runs real Debian alongside the stock software

A single image file keeps the Kindle's own system untouched

I used a chroot, which gives Debian its own root filesystem inside a single .ext3 image file. The Kindle doesn’t have to dual-boot into it, and I don't have to flash anything. A KUAL (Kindle Unified Application Launcher) extension mounts the image and chroots into it, while the Kindle’s own kernel keeps running underneath. The stock software stays untouched, so you don’t risk losing the e-reading experience. If I ever want Debian gone, I just delete the image file.

I found a tool on GitHub called kindle-linux-chroot that makes this straightforward. It builds ARMv7 images for Debian, Alpine, and Arch Linux ARM, and Void Linux should work too, even though it’s untested. It also includes a KUAL extension that launches the chroot, which saves me from stitching the mount commands together by hand. You do need a jailbroken Kindle with KUAL and kTerm first.

item.itunes:title: I used an ESP32 to map my Wi-Fi dead zones instead of walking around with my phone
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve stood in a corner of my house and suddenly lost wireless connectivity. I knew I couldn’t fully trust those Wi-Fi signal bars, so I'd shift my stance and wait for the bars to climb back up, hoping the connection would hold. But the number of bars never told me what I needed to do to use Wi-Fi without getting booted out.

I picked up a spare ESP32-S3 from an earlier project and decided to let it tell me about the weaker Wi-Fi zones in my house. I wasn’t expecting a professional-grade dead zone identifier, but I hoped for enough information to adjust my router, so the wireless connection reaches most corners.

I turned Wi-Fi signal into a home motion sensor using an ESP32, and it now controls my smart devices

It's what my Home Assistant server was missing all along

3
By  Ayush Pande

Wi-Fi analyzer apps on my phone rarely gave real answers

Signal bars don’t tell me where to stand

Like many, I surveyed my house using Wi-Fi signal bars on my phone and realized they're just indicators. They don’t give precise information. After trying three different Wi-Fi analyzer apps on the same phone, I stood in the same spot and found they disagreed: one claimed a strong connection, while another flagged the same corner as borderline. None of them noted where I was standing a few minutes ago. So, I couldn’t trust any single app to tell the whole story.

What I really wanted was a figure my router and wireless devices see, measured in decibels, not an estimate. So, instead of using my phone or a tablet, I wanted dedicated hardware that showed me the data plainly. A microcontroller can read that directly from its Wi-Fi chip. All I needed to do was pull that data from a microcontroller like an ESP32 and store it temporarily.

Picking the right ESP32 board is trickier than it sounds

I didn’t need Wi-Fi 6 or Zigbee radio specifically

While my drawer had a couple of ESP32 boards to choose from, I weighed the ESP32-S3 against the newer ESP32-C6. At first, the C6 seemed like a good choice, with Wi-Fi 6 and a built-in Zigbee radio. I liked the idea of using a second radio to step in if I ever walked into an absolute dead spot where my Wi-Fi gave out completely. That was my initial idea for mapping those spots accurately.

The idea sounded great, but it didn’t hold up on closer inspection. Reading Wi-Fi signal data off-board doesn’t care whether it has a Wi-Fi 6 chip. Also, relaying any information meant pairing it with a coordinator chip, which forwards the data. That was easier said than done, because getting the second radio to kick in when the Wi-Fi drops is tricky. For a simple job, I chose ESP32-S3 instead because of its mature tooling, and I wouldn’t have to debug any radio quirks on top of everything else.

ESP32-S3

ESP32-S3-N16R8 comes with a dual-core Xtensa LX7 microcontroller. It has 16MB of flash memory and 8MB of PSRAM with years of maturity to be ready for a variety of projects.

See at Amazon

Getting Wi-Fi signal strength data into Home Assistant

A small configuration file did the heavy lifting

It took a while to decide where the data would land, and I even evaluated a few versions of this project before settling on a simple option. At first, I considered running a web server to show the RSSI values, but it’d disappear the moment I closed the tab. That defeated the point of mapping anything.

I already had a Home Assistant instance running at home, and feeding the signal readings to it made more sense than building my own dashboard from scratch. A short YAML configuration file tells the ESP32-S3 to read the Wi-Fi signal strength, report it as a sensor, and from that point on, the numbers land somewhere I already check throughout the day anyway.

Recording room-by-room Wi-Fi data of the house

Helpers and a dashboard card helped close the loop

Flashing the ESPHome YAML configuration on the ESP32-S3 barely took a few minutes. To capture the board's RSSI data, I pulled everything into Home Assistant. I set up three separate sensors: one for the live reading, one for the running survey average, and one that holds the latest results for the room I’m standing in.

Next, I added a Wi-Fi Survey YAML configuration file that turns the board’s measurements into room-by-room survey data. Instead of a rigid, technical setup, I kept it simple, as the file includes a small script to start and stop Wi-Fi surveys and save the average RSSI values to the selected room’s helper.

On the Home Assistant dashboard, I used entity cards to create separate views for the live Wi-Fi signal, survey recording (with room and duration selection), live signal history, and a list of the latest result per room. All I had to do was visit a room, select the card, and start the survey to record that room's values.

I finally made my Wi-Fi snappier by changing the most ignored setting on my router

Your router's transmit power isn't supposed to be at the maximum level

11
By  Tanveer Singh

No more walking around with my phone

By the time I finished surveying all the rooms, I realized my kitchen and the other corner of the bedroom barely had wireless connectivity at all. The numbers were so low that I’d never trusted my phone’s bars to catch it. To find the dead spots, I used a cheap board, a short configuration file, a few helpers, and a couple of entity cards.

I already have the Home Assistant dashboard running on a tablet at home. But it gave me real data tied to every room, so I don't have to rely on my memory. If you’ve got a spare ESP32 from another project, this is a genuinely satisfying way to put it to work and find weak Wi-Fi zones in and around your home. It also means your next router or mesh node placement decision is based on real numbers instead of a hunch formed while waving your phone around.

ESP32
Brand
AITRIP
Connectivity Features
UART, USB

The ESP32 is a fantastic development board that combines solid specs with an affordable price. Despite being cheaper than Arduino and Raspberry Pi Pico, it outperforms most of its rivals. Plus, the ESP32 even has Wi-Fi and Bluetooth functionality built into every board, making it great for projects where you can't physically keep the microcontroller connected to your PC at all times.

See at Amazon

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I prefer to watch media with smooth visuals. Doesn't everybody? When you own a streaming box, you want to adjust the settings to get the best picture quality possible. However, Google TV streaming boxes turn off an essential setting by default, which prevents you from fixing uneven motion. So I adjusted one key option tucked away in the advanced display settings.

The Match Content Frame Rate setting lets my Google TV device match video frame rates instead of outputting a fixed rate. It delivers smoother, more consistent motion in movies and shows without constant manual switching. It's a key setting for avoiding judder in movies and shows.

Match Content Frame Rate

A vital setting that provides a smoother picture flow

This setting doesn't get enough attention. It improves picture quality by matching the HDMI output refresh rate to the video that's playing. With it disabled, everything displays at a fixed rate, such as 60Hz. With the matched frame rate, the goal is more consistent motion in the movies and shows I'm watching. It works really well in scenes with slow camera pans.

For instance, when I watch a movie filmed at 24 frames per second, a compatible app asks the Google TV box to switch its HDMI output refresh rate from 60Hz to 24Hz. It can even achieve fractional rates. Showing 24 fps at 60Hz requires alternating individual frames that remain on the screen.

That creates uneven motion known as "judder." Matching the output rate avoids judder and creates a more seamless, higher-quality picture. You generally don't need to adjust the TV's refresh rate manually; the Android TV box handles the output-rate switch, and the television displays the incoming signal.

Android TV is the least moddable version of Android — here's why

Despite sharing Android's roots, Android TV is surprisingly hard to mod

1
By  Abid Ahsan Shanto

It doesn't work with every app

Enabling it allows matching, but doesn't force every app to use it

Enabling the Match Content Frame Rate setting doesn't mean every app on the box must use it. Frame rate support on Android TV depends on the app. Popular streaming apps like Netflix support it on Android 12 or later, and you don't need to adjust any additional settings. Self-hosted media apps like Plex and Jellyfin offer controls to enable refresh rate matching. Check each app's video playback settings to see whether it enables it automatically or requires you to turn it on in-app.

For instance, in the Plex app, you can enable it in Advanced video and audio settings. In the Jellyfin app, you can find it under Settings > Advanced Playback > Refresh Rate Switching, or something similar depending on the client version. The video app you use may also name it something different, but similar. Still, even if I have to enable the option in a specific app, it's nicer than not having it at all, and I will gladly do it.

You also want to know which frame rate setting to use in each app. If it is set to scale on a device, it switches the refresh rate while retaining the display's output resolution, and the streaming box handles scaling. Scaling on the TV means the TV matches both the refresh rate and output resolution to the video. The TV handles scaling the resolution. When you see "match frame rate" settings in other apps, the wording differs, but the idea is the same. If you're not sure, play around with the settings until they work best for your viewing situation.

Brief black screen trade-off

Picture interruptions may be worth it

The seamless option might sound better, but it can prevent matching if your TV can't switch without interrupting the picture. When I change the setting to fix motion cadence, the app switches, and a brief black screen may appear as the HDMI signal switches. For instance, switching from 60Hz for the home screen to 24Hz for the video.

The TV needs a second to re-sync the new signal timing and goes black. The interruption usually lasts less than a moment, but the improved quality is worth it. A movie may look vivid and sharp but still have distracting motion, like a slow camera pan across a scene. So even with occasional short picture interruptions, I will gladly pay the price for less judder in crucial scenes.

That's why I enable the match setting before settling in to watch anything. It's a small adjustment, but it allows supported apps to choose the frame rate that best fits the content. It doesn't fix all picture issues, like network, transcoding, decoder, or other streaming box issues. But it addresses a specific problem in movies and shows. It makes motion in the picture feel more consistent than when it's off. The only thing I need to remember is to turn it on for specific apps that support it.

I changed these hidden Google TV settings to make my laggy TV feel brand new

Stop the stutter.

2
By  Parth Shah

The match content frame rate setting fixes motion cadence for movies and shows

You probably haven't thought much about this setting on your Google TV box. Likely because it isn't enabled, and you may chalk picture motion issues up to a slow processor or slow network connectivity. The next time you turn on your box, make a point to enable it. Experiment with different apps, and look for an option to enable it in the ones you use, if it exists. Remember, turning it on broadly doesn't mean all your apps will use it.

item.title: Smart Connect is the first thing I turn off on any new router, and my smart home is the reason
item.itunes:title: Smart Connect is the first thing I turn off on any new router, and my smart home is the reason
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When you own a smart home, random smart plugs go offline, bulbs refuse to report their state, and security cameras drop streams for no apparent reason. This means you constantly have to power-cycle devices.

It's easy to assume your Wi-Fi gear is failing or your IoT hardware is cheap, but the real enemy could be a factory-enabled router feature called Smart Connect (also called band steering). It's designed to simplify life for non-technical users by merging the 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands under a single SSID. Smart Connect treats low-power IoT clients like roaming smartphones, constantly trying to force them onto bands they actually can't handle. For those with a range of IoT hardware, this leads to constant dropouts.

The first thing you should do on any new router, if you have a smart home, is split your SSIDs and isolate your 2.4GHz band to bring permanent stability to your smart home.

5 router settings most people never touch that fixed my network problems

Lesser-known fixes for well-known problems

11
By  Chandraveer Mathur

What is Smart Connect?

Do you need it switched on?

Smart Connect, or band steering (depending on your router's make and model), can be extremely useful for most homes. If you're a non-technical household that just wants to use Wi-Fi to browse the internet on a few primary devices, it makes this much easier by combining the 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands and letting your devices switch between them effortlessly.

For more technical households, for example, those with smart home setups or home labs, this can be extremely frustrating. Most smart plugs, smart bulbs, switches, and robot vacuums support only 2.4GHz because they prioritize range and wall penetration over raw throughput. While the 5GHz band is faster, it simply doesn't penetrate walls as easily. With Smart Connect or band steering enabled, your router might keep trying to push these devices to 5GHz even though they don't support it.

Smart Connect uses algorithms to kick devices back and forth between bands based on signal metrics. When the router aggressively tries to steer a stubborn IoT client to 5GHz (which it doesn't even have the hardware for) or constantly probes it, the client can just drop the connection entirely, resulting in phantom offline states.

Splitting your SSIDs can remedy a lot of issues

Ol' reliable

Splitting your SSIDs is a simple way to restore sanity and reliability to your smart home devices. It might feel like an old-school method, but it remains the gold standard for so many power users to rectify this problem.

By giving your 2.4GHz network a dedicated SSID (for example, home network_IoT), this can ensure that your smart devices bind to the correct radio once and never get confused by router-initiated handoffs. All your IoT devices stay permanently bound to your 2.4GHz network, so you don't have to worry about compatibility issues when they move between bands.

On top of that, you preserve your high-speed channels for your primary devices, keeping your 5 GHz and 6 GHz bands exclusive to heavy-lifting clients like your laptops, phones, and media streamers. This can stop low-bitrate IoT beacon frames from clogging up high-performance airtime. Overall, you're also boosting your network's performance.

The simplest way is to log into your router's GUI, go to the advanced wireless settings, find the toggle for Smart Connect, Band Steering (or sometimes Smart Triband), and switch it off. After that, you should be able to create distinct SSIDs in those settings, too. Keep your bands separate, use your main network for roaming devices, and rename the 2.4GHz band specifically for that smart home gear.

While it's frustrating, you will likely have to reconnect all your IoT devices to the dedicated 2.4GHz SSID once you're done. Once it's done, you can rest assured knowing that they have a stable, unchanging connection path.

There are some issues you might have to overcome

But the fixes are simple

Unfortunately, many modern smart home setup apps (like Tuya smart bulb wizards or even Matter device onboarding) might refuse to configure if your phone is currently sitting on a 5GHz band while the device only sees 2.4GHz.

There are several workarounds to fix this issue. A simple option is to connect your phone to your 2.4GHz band temporarily while you set up your IoT devices. You can also temporarily use a guest network or segregate bands during initial pairing, then lock devices to your dedicated 2.4GHz SSID.

Once you set up your smart home this way, you may also run into issues when using features like casting. Your smart devices are on a separate IoT SSID, while your primary devices aren't, so they may not be able to communicate or see one another. You can fix this by enabling cross-network discovery. You can do this by enabling mDNS reflection or repeaters in your router settings. If you still have issues, you may need to configure your firewall rules to ensure it works.

Optimize your router to suit your home

Factory settings aren't always the best

Routers are designed to optimize general web browsing rather than understand the quirks of low-power microcontrollers inside smart switches. For more technically minded smart homes, you might benefit from taking manual control of your wireless bands, as this can fix instability. Disable Smart Connect and split your bands, and you'll watch your smart home finally stop dropping offline.
